question: Do the cited 1905 introduction and 1918 first-record claims establish the Philippine or Pasig origin of Monopterus albus, after tracing their source chain and historical taxonomic identity?

method.summary: Compared the 2021 Ame & Mayor article statement with Guerrero (2014), the unretrieved 1989 chapter citation, Fowler (1918) bibliographic records, a search-indexed OCR excerpt from Herre (1923), the DLSU dissertation abstract, a 2017 taxonomic conference paper, the NMNH Division of Fishes catalog, the USFWS 2025 risk-screening synthesis, and the relevant 2018 World Aquaculture secondary summary. Historical claims remain attributed and separate from contemporary Pasig population evidence. Added a collection-history and catalog screen: Sabaj (2020) documents a broad 1917 transfer of mostly Philippine PCM fish holdings to ANSP; Fowler’s later manuscript attaches nearby PCM references to different eel names; bounded ANSP/iDigBio name queries did not identify Fowler’s specimen.
accessNotes: Publisher-indexed text for the 2021 article and the online full text of Guerrero (2014) were reviewed. The 2021 article direct page returned HTTP 502; its publisher PDF result exposed the relevant article text.
The 1989 Juliano, Guerrero, and Ronquillo chapter was not retrieved; its citation and its role in the source chain were verified through bibliographic records only.
Fowler (1918) was verified bibliographically but its original Copeia pages were not retrieved or read.

Herre's 1923 page-125 OCR excerpt reports that Fowler's specimen was labeled only at the Philippine Islands level; the large scan was not visually reviewed, and this secondary account does not identify a waterbody or specimen number.

The public author-uploaded text of Chavez, Arcilla, and Carandang (2017), the DLSU dissertation abstract, and the USFWS 2025 PDF text were reviewed. A public NMNH Division of Fishes catalog query found 14 Philippine lot records with prior identification Monopterus albus and current catalog name Ophisternon bengalense, USNM 135196–135209. The paper does not publish accession numbers, so exact paper-to-catalog linkage remains inferred; see the focused crosswalk review.
No access control was bypassed and no source files, specimen records, images, or tables were retained.

Maini et al. (2018), pp. 59–60, were reviewed on the publisher site: the “since 1905” statement covers introduced freshwater fishes generally, while Table 1 is explicitly credited to Guerrero (2014) and lists Monopterus albus year as unknown. The table is secondary, not independent confirmation. UP MSI Library and UP Diliman service pages provide possible access/document-delivery routes for the cataloged book, but availability and copying terms are not confirmed; no inquiry was sent.

Sabaj (2020), Copeia 108(3), Supplemental Appendix 1, PCM entry (code 1920, p. 165), and the public BHL scan/OCR of Fowler’s circa 1930–1941 manuscript were reviewed. Fowler’s manuscript search returns PCM-associated examples under Pisoodonophis macgregori and Pisodonophis boro, not a direct Monopterus/Fluta alba match.

The ANSP official Ichthyology resources page and iDigBio public API result sets were checked. The exact Monopterus albus/ANSP query returned 25 records and no Philippines string in indexed fields; the Ophisternon bengalense/ANSP query returned five different records. The iDigBio set reports last modification in 2025. No ANSP staff contact was made.
method.reuseFinding: No item-specific republication permission was verified for the article, dissertation, conference paper, report, or historic bibliography. BioOne restricts its PDF use to personal, educational, and non-commercial use; BHL reports no known restrictions as determined by the scanning institution. Only concise attributed research summaries are retained, and no independent legal determination was made.

sourceFindings.scope: The article states that Monopterus albus was introduced to the Philippines in 1905 for aquaculture and cites Juliano et al. (1989) and Guerrero (2014). Its field study concerns rice fields in Cagayan Valley.
sourceFindings.limits: The 1989 chapter was not retrieved. The article provides no Pasig or NCR specimen evidence, and the 1905 statement cannot be independently traced to an eel-specific dated record from the reviewed chain.
sourceFindings.attribution: Retain 1905 as Ame and Mayor's statement, not as a verified Philippine-wide or Pasig-specific introduction year.

sourceFindings.scope: The article title covers introduced fish in the Philippines from 1905 to 2013; its introduction says Juliano et al. reported 34 freshwater fish introductions over 1905–1988. The Monopterus albus table row lists Malaysia as origin, year as unknown, and culture/natural breeding/wild status codes.
sourceFindings.limits: The 1905–2013 and 1905–1988 ranges are periods for broad reviews, not an eel-specific date. The table does not substantiate 1905 for Monopterus.
sourceFindings.attribution: Use the table's unknown year when describing what Guerrero (2014) reports; do not transfer the review's start year to this species.

sourceFindings.scope: Bibliographic records identify the cited chapter as pp. 83–90 in Exotic Aquatic Organisms in Asia and confirm its relevance to Philippine fish introductions.
sourceFindings.limits: The chapter text was not obtained. It is unknown whether it gives a species-specific 1905 date, a broader national introduction period, or any specimen/source detail for Monopterus.
sourceFindings.attribution: Keep the chapter as an unresolved source-chain lead; do not claim it confirms the 1905 eel date.

sourceFindings.scope: Bibliographic records identify Fowler's A List of Philippine Fishes in Copeia 58 (1918), pp. 62–65. Later works cite this list as an early Philippine Monopterus albus inventory.
sourceFindings.limits: The original pages were not reviewed. A publication or inventory year is not necessarily the date an animal arrived, and the cited bibliographic record contains no Pasig locality or specimen identifier.
sourceFindings.attribution: Describe 1918 only as the year of a cited historical inventory unless original specimen and collection metadata are located.

sourceFindings.scope: A search-indexed OCR excerpt attributed to Herre's page 125 says he had not personally seen Philippine specimens, reports the eel via Fowler, and says the Fowler specimen in the Philadelphia Commercial Museum carried only a broad Philippine Islands label; the footnote points to Fowler's 1918 Copeia page 62.
sourceFindings.limits: The page image was not visually checked, Herre is a later secondary source for Fowler, and the excerpt provides no waterbody, collection date, catalog number, or link to the 14 Smithsonian lots.
sourceFindings.attribution: Keep this as provisional OCR-derived historical context, not a direct Fowler transcription, NCR/Pasig occurrence, or introduction date.

sourceFindings.scope: The dissertation abstract says the eel was introduced and first recorded in the Philippines in 1918; it reports opportunistic samples from four Luzon sites.
sourceFindings.limits: The abstract does not name the four sites. The full dissertation was not reviewed, and its summary does not establish the identity or status of a Pasig population.
sourceFindings.attribution: Retain the 1918 wording as the dissertation abstract's claim, distinct from an independently verified introduction date.

sourceFindings.scope: The 2017 paper's abstract says the first inventory was in 1917, while its main text describes Fowler's 1918 inventory. It reports that 14 Philippine lots once catalogued as Monopterus albus were reclassified as Ophisternon bengalensis, based on a personal communication with Smithsonian curator David Smith; the authors say they examined sample Smithsonian specimens in 2016.
sourceFindings.limits: The paper prints no catalog or accession identifiers, locality-by-lot table, determination dates, or direct Smithsonian link for those 14 lots. The 1917/1918 discrepancy remains unexplained. A separate NMNH search returns exactly 14 Philippine Specimen/Lot entries with prior identification Monopterus albus and current catalog name Ophisternon bengalense; the count and name crosswalk strongly corroborate the report, but the paper does not explicitly identify USNM 135196–135209 as its set.
sourceFindings.attribution: Treat the 14-lot count and taxonomic reclassification as strongly corroborated by the museum catalog while keeping exact paper-to-catalog-set linkage inferred. It cautions against treating the historical name as confirmed modern Monopterus.

sourceFindings.scope: The public NMNH Division of Fishes catalog has 14 Philippine Specimen/Lot records, USNM 135196–135209, each with current catalog name Ophisternon bengalense and prior identification Monopterus albus. The records are dated March–August 1908 and list Manila Market or Malabon Market locality wording; all list the Albatross Philippine Expedition, 1907–1910, and raw NMNH field acqln=065731 (field label not interpreted).
sourceFindings.limits: The catalog market labels are not capture-site evidence and do not identify a river, lake, or other source water. NMNH states that only slightly over half of its holdings are online and geographic retrieval fields may be inaccurate. No direct Fowler specimen or Commercial Museum transfer link is present in the reviewed records.
sourceFindings.attribution: This is primary catalog support for a 14-lot historical name crosswalk. The agreement with the 2017 paper is strong but the paper omits the accession numbers, so their exact correspondence is not explicit. It establishes neither introduction timing nor present-day occurrence, habitat, native status, or invasiveness.

sourceFindings.scope: The 2025 synthesis describes Monopterus albus as a likely species complex, reproduces the IUCN Philippines native-range classification, and separately summarizes swamp eels brought from Malaysia for aquaculture. It says those later introductions have unknown dates and counts but are presumed after about 2000; it also attributes a 2008 Nagadacan rivers introduction account to northern Luzon residents.
sourceFindings.limits: These are attributed secondary accounts and do not resolve the historical Fowler specimen, identify which taxon-complex members were moved, or establish any Pasig occurrence or origin.
sourceFindings.attribution: Keep the later aquaculture/community accounts distinct from the 1905 and 1918 claims and do not generalize them to NCR.

sourceFindings.scope: The publisher-hosted magazine article says 62 freshwater fish species had been introduced into Philippine waters since 1905, citing Juliano et al. (1989), Joshi (2006), and Guerrero (2014). Its Table 1 explicitly credits Guerrero (2014) and lists Monopterus albus origin as Malaysia and year as unknown (U).
sourceFindings.limits: This is a secondary summary. Its since-1905 statement is an aggregate period, and its Monopterus row reproduces the Guerrero (2014) table rather than providing an independent dated record. Only pages 59–60 were read; the 1989 chapter remains unavailable in the reviewed public digital routes.
sourceFindings.attribution: Use only to clarify that the secondary review period begins in 1905 while the cited table leaves the species year unknown; it does not establish an eel-specific 1905 date, specimen occurrence, or Pasig origin.

sourceFindings.scope: Sabaj (2020), Supplemental Appendix 1, PCM entry, states that extant PCM fishes, mostly from the Philippines, were transferred to ANSP in 1917.
sourceFindings.limits: Collection-level transfer note only; it gives no specimen/catalog list and does not name Fowler’s eel. Herre’s 1923 account still attributes Fowler’s specimen to the Philadelphia Commercial Museum, leaving a custody/timing discrepancy.
sourceFindings.attribution: Use as a plausible historical collection route to ANSP, not as evidence that Fowler’s specific specimen was transferred or survives there.

sourceFindings.scope: Fowler’s public BHL archival manuscript has PCM references within other named eel entries (Pisoodonophis macgregori and Pisodonophis boro). Bounded OCR searches for Monopterus, Fluta alba, Synbranchus, and eel produced no matches.
sourceFindings.limits: The manuscript is later and unpublished; the OCR can miss text. The two PCM references are to different named taxa and give no catalog number for the eel discussed by Herre.
sourceFindings.attribution: Exclude the nearby PCM passages as false matches to the swamp-eel specimen; retain the manuscript only as collection-history context.

sourceFindings.scope: ANSP’s official collection-resource page identifies its departmental fish database and states that its staff provide information on holdings and that collection managers are the route for current records.
sourceFindings.limits: The public site and its general description do not establish any specific Fowler/PCM accession; the portal page was indexed, but its database redirect was not independently queried through the text retrieval interface.
sourceFindings.attribution: Use only to document a future public search/holdings route; no contact or request was made.

sourceFindings.scope: The ANSP institution-code query for Monopterus albus returned 25 rows with no “Philippines” text in the indexed record fields. The separate Ophisternon bengalense query returned five ANSP rows, including one purchased Orion, Bataan record from 1923 and four Malabon entries from 1930.
sourceFindings.limits: iDigBio’s indexed resultset is dated 2025; current-name queries miss unindexed, differently named, uncatalogued, or historical files. The Ophisternon catalog entries have no PCM/Fowler identifier and are not shown to be the same specimen or taxon.
sourceFindings.attribution: This bounded screen found no match; it does not establish absence from ANSP or connect any returned record to Fowler’s eel.

sourceChainAssessment.1905Claim: Reported by Ame and Mayor (2021), which cites Juliano et al. (1989) and Guerrero (2014). Guerrero’s directly reviewed table records the Monopterus year as unknown, and the 1989 chapter remains unread. Maini et al. (2018) repeats a broad since-1905 period for introduced freshwater fishes, citing those reviews, and its table—explicitly credited to Guerrero (2014)—also lists the eel year as unknown. These secondary sources do not verify 1905 as a Monopterus-specific introduction year.
sourceChainAssessment.1917Or1918Claim: Fowler's 1918 publication is cited as an early Philippine inventory; the 2017 paper has an internal 1917/1918 discrepancy, and Nisperos (2022) calls 1918 the first country record. Herre's 1923 search-indexed OCR says Fowler's specimen was broadly labeled Philippine Islands, but the scan page is unverified and no waterbody or collection date is supplied. NMNH catalog dates place the 14 market-labeled lots in 1908, before Fowler's publication, but do not identify their source waters or prove a species introduction date. None of these dates identifies a modern Pasig eel.
sourceChainAssessment.historicalIdentity: The 2017 paper's report of 14 Philippine Monopterus-labelled lots reclassified to Ophisternon bengalensis is strongly corroborated by 14 public NMNH records, USNM 135196–135209, whose prior identification is Monopterus albus and current catalog name is Ophisternon bengalense. Because the paper prints no accession numbers, identifying those records as the exact reported set remains a strong count/name inference rather than an explicit cross-reference. The catalog localities are Manila/Malabon market labels and cannot be treated as capture waters or as Fowler's specimen. The USFWS synthesis further notes that M. albus as historically used encompasses a probable complex.
sourceChainAssessment.laterIntroductionAccounts: The USFWS summary describes later Malaysian aquaculture introductions, presumed after about 2000, plus a locally attributed 2008 Nagadacan account. These may concern different populations or taxa and do not adjudicate the Pasig record.
sourceChainAssessment.resolution: The dates are not a simple contradiction: 1905 is framed as an introduction date, while 1918 is framed as a first inventory/record date. However, the 1905 date is not verified in its cited source chain; the 1918 historic name is taxonomically contested; and later introductions are also reported. Separately, Sabaj (2020) documents a broad 1917 PCM-to-ANSP fish-collection route, but no catalog number or transfer ledger links Fowler’s eel to ANSP. Herre’s 1923 holder attribution and the bounded public catalog searches leave the individual specimen identity and custody unresolved; the origin and identity of the Pasig fish remain unresolved.
sourceChainAssessment.decision: Do not label the Pasig fish native, introduced, invasive, or confirmed as Monopterus albus from this source chain. Do not add an occurrence row or public species projection.
sourceChainAssessment.museumTransferRoute: Sabaj (2020) documents a broad 1917 transfer of extant PCM fishes, mostly from the Philippines, to ANSP. This establishes a possible custody route for Philippine fishes as a group, not a transfer record for Fowler’s eel. Herre’s 1923 account still names the Philadelphia Commercial Museum as the specimen holder, and no specimen number reconciles that statement with the 1917 transfer.
sourceChainAssessment.fowlerSpecimenCatalogScreen: A bounded ANSP/iDigBio query returned 25 ANSP records indexed as Monopterus albus, none with Philippines text in their indexed fields, plus five ANSP Ophisternon bengalense records. Those Ophisternon records have unrelated catalog numbers/locality/date fields and no PCM/Fowler accession link. Fowler’s later BHL manuscript shows PCM references under Pisoodonophis macgregori and Pisodonophis boro, not a direct swamp-eel match. These non-matches do not prove the historical specimen is absent from ANSP.

scopeAndReuseDecision.decision: Research-only historical source-chain review. No public species assertion, occurrence row, image, diet, geometry, catchability, rule, or app projection.
scopeAndReuseDecision.paperToCatalogSetLinkage: strong count-and-name agreement; exact accession linkage inferred, not explicit

nonClaims: The review does not establish that the first eel introduction to the Philippines occurred in 1905, 1918, or after 2000.
No claim is made that all Philippine or Pasig swamp eels are native or introduced.

USNM 135196–135209 strongly match the 2017 paper's reported 14-lot count and prior/current names, but the paper does not print their catalog numbers; exact identity with the authors' set is not explicit.
The Manila and Malabon market locality labels do not establish the original capture water or habitat of the 14 catalog lots.
No historical specimen from Fowler is linked to Pasig, NCR, or a named waterbody.
Herre's 1923 OCR excerpt has not been checked against the scan image and its broad Philippine Islands label does not establish a waterbody.
Four unnamed Luzon dissertation sampling sites are not assigned to NCR or Pasig.
No present-day presence, abundance, season, fishing legality, safety, diet, or bait recommendation is made.

Maini et al. (2018) gives 1905 only as an aggregate starting point for introduced freshwater fishes; its Guerrero-attributed table marks Monopterus year unknown and is not independent species-specific date evidence.
Sabaj (2020) documents a collection-level PCM fish transfer to ANSP in 1917; this does not prove Fowler’s specific eel was transferred.
No ANSP/iDigBio catalog record or accession number was linked to Fowler’s eel. A bounded non-hit in current indexed records is not evidence that the specimen is absent from ANSP.
Fowler manuscript passages mentioning the Philadelphia Commercial Museum under Pisoodonophis macgregori and Pisodonophis boro are different named taxa and are not evidence for the swamp-eel specimen.
nextActions: If needed, obtain and read Juliano, Guerrero, and Ronquillo (1989), pp. 83–90, through the UP Diliman Marine Science Institute Library route after confirming current availability, public access/document-delivery eligibility, fees, and permitted copying conditions; trace any eel-specific date to underlying primary records.

Continue seeking permitted access to Fowler (1918), page 62, and, if direct identification is still needed, seek a PCM-to-ANSP transfer ledger or catalog crosswalk for the specific Philadelphia Commercial Museum specimen; no match is established by the collection-level transfer note or bounded aggregator queries.
Seek the Pasig fish assessment table, specimen vouchers, station localities, collection dates, and any diagnostic or genetic methods before resolving its taxon or population origin.
Continue NCR freshwater, brackish, and marine evidence discovery; this review does not change regional baseline or completion status.
